what-is-risk-management.title: What is risk management?
what-is-risk-management.label: Explainer · Foundations · Beginner
what-is-risk-management.desc: Risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, the risk management loop, and the ways to respond to a risk.

transcript.visual: Title card: What is risk management? The loop every risk process follows.
A statement appears: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives.
captions: The international guideline ISO 31000 describes risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives. No objective, no risk.

transcript.visual: Three cards compare a risk, an issue and an incident, each with a payment system example.
captions: A risk might happen. An issue is a problem that exists now. An incident is something that has already happened.

transcript.visual: A cycle of six steps appears one by one: set the context, identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, monitor and review. In the centre: communicate, consult and record at every step.
captions: Most frameworks follow a loop. First, set the context: the objective, the scope and the criteria for judging risks.
Then identify what could happen, analyse how likely and how severe it is, and evaluate whether it is acceptable.
Treat the risks that aren't acceptable. Then monitor and review, because risks and controls change.
Identifying, analysing and evaluating together are called risk assessment. Communication runs through every step.

transcript.visual: Five cards show the responses: avoid, reduce, share, accept and pursue.
captions: There are only a few ways to respond: avoid, reduce, share or accept a risk, or pursue an opportunity. Most real cases use a mix.

transcript.visual: A statement: the aim isn't zero risk, it's taking the right risks knowingly.
captions: Every organisation takes risks to achieve anything. Risk management makes those choices deliberate, and keeps the rest at a level it can live with.

transcript.visual: A statement about the APRA requirement for a risk management framework under CPS 220 and SPS 220.
captions: For regulated financial institutions, risk management isn't optional. It is a legal requirement overseen by APRA.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

breach-reporting-clocks.title: Breach reporting: from awareness to report
breach-reporting-clocks.label: Explainer · Compliance · Intermediate
breach-reporting-clocks.desc: Why the awareness date matters, the main reporting clocks, and how one event can trigger several regimes.

transcript.visual: Title card: Breach reporting, from awareness to report.
A statement: reporting clocks run from awareness, not from certainty.
captions: Most reporting deadlines start when the organisation becomes aware, not when the investigation is finished.

transcript.visual: A timeline from awareness through 24 hours, 72 hours, 3 business days and 30 days, each labelled with the regime that applies. Scale is illustrative.
captions: Different regimes run on different clocks. For APRA-regulated entities, some notifications fall due within 24 or 72 hours.
Suspicious matter reports to AUSTRAC are due within three business days, and ASIC reportable situations within 30 calendar days.

transcript.visual: A flow showing the steps to decide whether a breach is a reportable situation for ASIC.
captions: For AFS and credit licensees, a significant breach of a core obligation must be reported. Some breaches are automatically significant.

transcript.visual: A statement: one event can trigger several regimes at once.
captions: Keep one tracker of every regime that might apply, its test, its deadline and who owns it. Record decisions not to report, too.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

controls-design-and-testing.title: Controls: design, operation and testing
controls-design-and-testing.label: Explainer · Risk management · Intermediate
controls-design-and-testing.desc: Preventive, detective and corrective controls, design versus operating effectiveness, and how controls are tested.

transcript.visual: Title card: Controls, design, operation and testing.
Three cards: preventive, detective and corrective controls with examples.
captions: A control is anything that keeps a risk within appetite. Controls can prevent, detect or correct problems.

transcript.visual: Two cards compare design effectiveness and operating effectiveness.
captions: Testing asks two separate questions. First: is the control well designed? Would it work if performed as described?
Second: did it actually operate, consistently, over the whole period? A well-designed control that isn't performed does nothing.

transcript.visual: A bar chart ranks test methods from inquiry, the weakest, to reperformance, the strongest.
captions: Not all evidence is equal. Asking someone is weakest; inspecting records or reperforming the control is much stronger.

transcript.visual: A flow from test to exception, root cause, and action with validation.
captions: Every exception needs a root cause and an action. The issue is closed only when someone independent confirms the fix works.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

cps-230-in-90-seconds.title: CPS 230 in 90 seconds
cps-230-in-90-seconds.label: Explainer · Standards · Intermediate
cps-230-in-90-seconds.desc: APRA's operational risk standard: operational risk management, business continuity and service providers.

transcript.visual: Title card: CPS 230 in 90 seconds.
A statement that CPS 230 has been in force since 1 July 2025.
captions: CPS 230 is APRA's cross-industry standard for operational risk. It replaced several older standards on continuity and outsourcing.

transcript.visual: Three cards: operational risk management, business continuity and service providers.
captions: First, manage operational risk end to end: assess risks, maintain and test controls, and handle incidents.
Second, keep critical operations running through disruption, within tolerance levels approved by the board.
Third, manage the risks of relying on service providers, including the providers they rely on.

transcript.visual: Three cards combine into tolerance levels: maximum disruption, maximum data loss and minimum service levels.
captions: For each critical operation, the board approves tolerance levels: maximum disruption, maximum data loss and minimum service levels.

transcript.visual: A timeline of CPS 230 notifications: 24 hours, 72 hours and 20 business days.
captions: APRA must be told within 24 hours of a disruption outside tolerance, and within 72 hours of a material operational risk incident.

transcript.visual: A statement: the board is ultimately accountable.
captions: Accountability sits with the board and senior management, not with the service provider or the risk team.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

data-breach-response.title: Data breaches: contain, assess, notify
data-breach-response.label: Explainer · Compliance · Intermediate
data-breach-response.desc: How the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme works: containing a breach, assessing serious harm, and notifying the OAIC and individuals.

transcript.visual: Title card: Data breaches. Contain, assess, notify.
A statement defining a data breach.
captions: A data breach can be a cyber attack, but also an email sent to the wrong person or a lost laptop.

transcript.visual: A four-step cycle: contain, assess, notify and review.
captions: First, contain it: stop the breach and try to recover the information. Quick action can reduce the harm.
Then assess. If there are reasonable grounds to suspect an eligible breach, assess it quickly, generally within 30 days.
If an eligible data breach has happened, notify the OAIC and affected individuals as soon as practicable.
Finally, review what happened and fix the cause, so the same thing doesn't happen again.

transcript.visual: Three conditions combine to make an eligible data breach.
captions: It is eligible if serious harm is likely and remedial action hasn't prevented it. Tax file numbers and identity documents raise the risk.

transcript.visual: A statement about the separate CPS 234 notification to APRA.
captions: Privacy notification isn't the only clock. Check every regime that might apply.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

denominator-effect.title: The denominator effect in super
denominator-effect.label: Explainer · Risk management · Advanced
denominator-effect.desc: How falling listed markets, slow-moving unlisted valuations and member outflows push up the share of unlisted assets, and why it matters for fairness.

transcript.visual: Title card: The denominator effect, liquidity and fairness in super.
A statement: your unlisted share can grow without buying anything.
captions: Unlisted assets like property and infrastructure are revalued slowly. Listed markets reprice every day.

transcript.visual: Three stacked bars. Before: cash 5, listed 70, unlisted 25, unlisted share 25 percent. After the market fall: cash 5, listed 49, unlisted 23.75, unlisted share 30.5 percent. After outflows of 15 paid from liquid assets: liquid 39, unlisted 23.75, unlisted share 37.8 percent, above a dashed line marking the 30 percent maximum.
captions: Start with $100: $5 in cash, $70 in listed assets and $25 unlisted, against a strategic maximum of 30% unlisted.
Listed markets fall 30%, but unlisted valuations fall only 5% so far. Unlisted is now about 30.5% of the option.
Members switch and leave, and $15 is paid out from liquid assets. Unlisted is now about 37.8%, well above the maximum.

transcript.visual: A statement: stale valuations can transfer value between members.
captions: That is why liquidity management and valuation governance are linked: both are about paying members fairly.

transcript.visual: Three cards: stress test, revalue and plan.
captions: SPS 530 requires liquidity stress testing at least annually, as part of a comprehensive stress testing program.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

dominant-message.title: Misleading conduct: the dominant message test
dominant-message.label: Explainer · Compliance · Advanced
dominant-message.desc: How courts decide whether a communication is misleading: the overall impression, the audience, the dominant message and the greenwashing cases.

transcript.visual: Title card: Misleading conduct, the dominant message test.
A statement: a statement can be true word for word and still mislead.
captions: The law asks what overall impression ordinary members of the audience would take away, and whether it is wrong.

transcript.visual: Four cards in sequence: audience, message, reaction and truth.
captions: Identify the audience, then the message it receives, including what is implied and what dominates.
Ask whether ordinary, reasonable members of that audience would be led into error, ignoring extreme or fanciful reactions.

transcript.visual: A mock social media ad with a large headline, Australia's top performing Balanced fund, 11.2% returns, and tiny fine print. A highlight marks the headline as the dominant message and the fine print as easily missed.
captions: Here the headline says the fund is the top performer. The qualification is in tiny print at the bottom.
In ACCC v TPG (2013), the High Court held that fine print may not correct a misleading dominant message.

transcript.visual: Four cards summarise the Puxu, Campomar, Miller v BMW and TPG cases.
captions: High Court cases built the tests: the whole context, the ordinary member of the audience, misleading silence and the dominant message.

transcript.visual: A bar chart of ASIC's first three greenwashing civil penalties: Mercer $11.3 million, Vanguard $12.9 million and Active Super $10.5 million.
captions: The greenwashing cases show product claims must match what the product actually holds, across every channel.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

far-accountability.title: FAR: who is accountable for what
far-accountability.label: Explainer · Governance · Intermediate
far-accountability.desc: The Financial Accountability Regime: accountable persons, statements and maps, obligations and deferred pay.

transcript.visual: Title card: The Financial Accountability Regime. Who is accountable for what.
A statement: for every significant part of the business, a named senior person who is accountable.
captions: After the Royal Commission, it was often hard to say who was responsible when things went wrong. FAR addresses that.

transcript.visual: Three linked cards: accountable persons, accountability statements and the accountability map.
captions: Each accountable person has a statement of their responsibilities, and the entity keeps a map showing who holds what.

transcript.visual: Three cards list the obligations of accountable persons.
captions: Accountable persons must act with honesty, integrity and care, deal openly with the regulators, and take reasonable steps.

transcript.visual: A statement about deferred remuneration under FAR.
captions: Consequences are real: deferred pay can be reduced, and regulators can disqualify accountable persons.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

remediation.title: Remediation: putting people back
remediation.label: Explainer · Compliance · Intermediate
remediation.desc: The six stages of consumer remediation under ASIC RG 277, and the principles behind them.

transcript.visual: Title card: Remediation, putting people back where they should be.
A statement: return people to the position they would have been in.
captions: When conduct causes loss, ASIC's guidance in RG 277 expects licensees to put affected people back where they would have been.

transcript.visual: Six stages in a row: identify, scope, calculate, tell, pay and close.
captions: Start as soon as there are reasonable grounds to suspect loss. Don't wait for complaints or the regulator.
Scope in everyone who was or may have been affected. Where data is missing, use assumptions that favour consumers.
Communicate clearly, pay people, and close only when the cause is fixed and payments are checked.

transcript.visual: Three cards: beneficial assumptions, free and easy, governance.
captions: Three principles apply throughout: beneficial assumptions, making it free and easy, and strong governance.

transcript.visual: A statement about residual amounts under RG 277.
captions: RG 277 also covers small amounts owed to former customers and money that can't be returned.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

risk-appetite.title: Risk appetite: from board statement to daily decisions
risk-appetite.label: Explainer · Risk management · Intermediate
risk-appetite.desc: Risk capacity, appetite, triggers and limits, and how appetite cascades into decisions and reporting.

transcript.visual: Title card: Risk appetite, from board statement to daily decisions.
A statement asking how much risk the organisation is prepared to take.
captions: Risk appetite is the board's answer to a simple question with hard consequences.

transcript.visual: A horizontal scale with markers for within appetite, amber trigger, red limit and risk capacity.
captions: Picture a scale of increasing risk. Appetite is where the board wants risk to sit, well inside what it could survive.
A trigger gives early warning. A limit marks the tolerance the board has set. Capacity is the most the organisation could bear.

transcript.visual: Four layers from the board statement down to day-to-day decisions, with arrows for cascading down and reporting up.
captions: Appetite only works if it cascades: from the board's statement to tolerances, business limits and key risk indicators.
And information has to flow back up, so the board can see whether the organisation is operating within appetite.

transcript.visual: Three cards describe common risk appetite pitfalls.
captions: Watch for three pitfalls: “zero appetite” for unavoidable risks, metrics that don't match the words, and statements that change nothing.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

swiss-cheese-and-fault-trees.title: Root causes: Swiss cheese and fault trees
swiss-cheese-and-fault-trees.label: Explainer · Risk management · Advanced
swiss-cheese-and-fault-trees.desc: Why “human error” is rarely a root cause, James Reason's Swiss cheese model, and how fault trees show which controls matter most.

transcript.visual: Title card: Root causes, Swiss cheese and fault trees.
A statement: human error is rarely a root cause.
captions: Many incident reviews stop at the person. Good analysis keeps asking why until it reaches causes the organisation can fix.

transcript.visual: Four slices of cheese labelled design, controls, supervision and people, each with holes. The holes line up and an arrow passes through all four to an incident.
captions: Psychologist James Reason pictured defences as slices of Swiss cheese. Every layer has holes.
An incident happens when holes in several layers line up. Many holes are latent conditions built in long before.

transcript.visual: A fault tree. Top event: members charged the wrong fee, 22 percent a year. Below an OR gate, two paths. Path one: configuration error 30 percent AND reconciliation misses it 60 percent, giving 18 percent. Path two: override error 50 percent AND review misses it 10 percent, giving 5 percent.
captions: A fault tree works down from the event. Each path needs a cause AND a failed control. Either path causes the event.
Through an AND gate, probabilities multiply. So a reliable detective control can matter as much as preventing the cause.

transcript.visual: Two cards compare weaker actions, such as reminders, with stronger actions, such as automation and independent checks.
captions: Strong actions change the system. Then check the fix works, and look for the same cause elsewhere.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

three-lines-model.title: The Three Lines model
three-lines-model.label: Explainer · Foundations · Beginner
three-lines-model.desc: Who does what in managing risk: the first line, the second line, internal audit and the governing body.

transcript.visual: Title card: The Three Lines model. Who does what in managing risk.
A statement: everyone manages risk, the question is who does what.
captions: The Three Lines model is a widely used way of describing roles in risk management and assurance.

transcript.visual: Four layers appear from top to bottom: governing body, first line, second line and third line, each with a description.
captions: At the top sits the governing body, usually the board. It is accountable to stakeholders and oversees everything below.
The first line is the business itself. The people who serve customers own their risks and run the controls day to day.
The second line is specialists in risk and compliance. They set frameworks, give advice, monitor and challenge.
The third line is internal audit. It gives the board independent assurance that the whole system is working.

transcript.visual: Two cards compare the old three lines of defence with the 2020 roles-based model.
captions: The 2020 version dropped the “defence” language and treats the lines as roles that work together, not rigid walls.

transcript.visual: A statement: owning a risk and checking it are different jobs.
captions: A common failure: blurred roles. When the people who check a control also run it, independent challenge disappears.

transcript.visual: A flow of four boxes shows the lines applied to paying a super benefit.
captions: In practice: the business runs the payment controls, risk tests them, internal audit reviews both, and the board oversees.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

unit-pricing-errors.title: Unit pricing errors: who wins and who loses
unit-pricing-errors.label: Explainer · Sectors · Advanced
unit-pricing-errors.desc: How a super fund unit price is built, how a pricing error moves value between members, and the debate over materiality thresholds.

transcript.visual: Title card: Unit pricing errors, who wins and who loses.
An equation: assets minus liabilities equals net asset value, divided by units on issue equals the unit price.
captions: A unit price is the option's net assets divided by the units on issue. Every contribution, switch and withdrawal uses it.

transcript.visual: A statement: correct price $1.2000, price used $1.2100.
captions: Suppose an error in a valuation makes the price about 0.83% too high for a week. Who is affected?

transcript.visual: Three cards: joining members lose, leaving members gain, staying members pay.
captions: People investing at the inflated price get fewer units than they should.
People leaving are paid too much, and members who stay bear the cost.

transcript.visual: A statement about the 0.30% materiality threshold and the debate about it.
captions: Whether relying on a materiality threshold fits trustees' duties is a live question. Small errors across many members add up.

transcript.visual: A flow: contain, quantify, correct, fix the cause.
captions: Correct every affected transaction, restore the option, decide who bears the cost, and fix the control that failed.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.

who-regulates-what.title: Who regulates what in Australia
who-regulates-what.label: Explainer · Foundations · Beginner
who-regulates-what.desc: Australia's twin peaks model, and the other regulators that cut across financial services.

transcript.visual: Title card: Who regulates what in Australia.
A flow from Parliament to Treasury to regulators to courts and AFCA.
captions: Parliament makes the laws. Regulators administer and enforce them, often by making more detailed rules and guidance.

transcript.visual: Two cards: APRA for financial soundness and ASIC for conduct and disclosure.
captions: Financial services use a twin peaks model. APRA looks after the financial soundness of banks, insurers and super funds.
ASIC looks after conduct and disclosure: how firms treat customers, markets and investors.

transcript.visual: Five cards: AUSTRAC, OAIC, ACCC, RBA and ATO with their roles.
captions: Other bodies cut across many industries: AUSTRAC, the OAIC, the ACCC, the Reserve Bank and the ATO.

transcript.visual: A statement that a large super fund answers to several regulators at once.
captions: Most financial institutions deal with several regulators at once, which is why mapping obligations matters.

transcript.visual: End card with the page title, web address and a general information disclaimer.
